metadata.title: Expectancy-value-cost motivational profiles in biology and physics: Their relations with gender, self-reported satisfaction of needs, and learning behavior

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a voluntary school-based sample in Estonia (34 schools) with students assessed in computer labs during regular school days. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or any student/sampling weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and does not describe replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the analyses are person-oriented (latent profile analysis with TYPE = COMPLEX clustered by classroom) and subsequent group comparisons in Mplus, the paper does not provide a survey-weight variable to apply for population-representative inference. Therefore, weighting is treated as not applied/undocumented, and results should be interpreted as describing the participating schools/students rather than producing nationally representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are motivational belief profiles and self-reported learning behavior/teacher-perception scales derived from questionnaire items and a scenario-based strategy task, not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA PV framework. Missing-data handling is not reported in the provided text; this is a reporting gap because latent profile analysis and subsequent BCH-based comparisons can be sensitive to how missing responses are treated (e.g., listwise deletion vs. model-based handling).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 8th- and 9th-grade students from 34 schools in Estonia who participated in the project “Developing tools for assessing science-related motivation”. The analytic sample comprised 888 eighth-grade and 614 ninth-grade students (1502 total), including 871 students in Estonian-speaking schools and 633 in Russian-speaking schools. Students completed the computer-based assessment in April–May 2022 (about 45 minutes) in Estonian or Russian depending on school language; the manuscript does not specify additional exclusions beyond the reported final sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA (not used); Estonia upper middle school (Grade 8-9) biology & physics motivational profiles (2022 assessment)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent profile analysis fit indices used to select 6 profiles: AIC/BIC/aBIC decreased with more profiles; chosen 6-profile solution with highest entropy (0.81) and non-significant VLMR for 6 vs 5 (VLMR = 0.199). Profile sizes: Moderate 618 (41%), Adaptive 455 (30%), Maladaptive 135 (9%), Biology-Adaptive 131 (9%), Physics-Adaptive 120 (8%), Indifferent 43 (3%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Estonia Grade 8–9 biology and physics assessment the study leveraged biology and physics expectancy/value/cost indicators to identify latent motivational profile membership, finding that six distinct profiles emerged (Moderate, Adaptive, Maladaptive, Biology-Adaptive, Physics-Adaptive, Indifferent) with most students in subject-general profiles. This indicates that most upper-middle-school students have not yet formed strong cross-subject EVC hierarchies between biology and physics, while a smaller but meaningful subgroup shows subject-specific motivational patterns that may require targeted support.

main_findings.dataset_used: Estonia upper middle school (Grade 8-9) biology & physics motivational profiles (2022 assessment)
main_findings.target_variable: Reported use of deep learning strategies across profiles
main_findings.performance_metrics: Omnibus differences across profiles were significant (Table 4): Reported deep learning strategy use χ2 = 124.97 (p < .001). Patterns: Deep strategy use was highest in Adaptive (M = 3.25) and lowest in Indifferent (M = 1.77). Maladaptive reported lower deep strategy use than Moderate and Biology-Adaptive. Additional analysis (Self-reported task persistence across profiles): Omnibus differences across profiles were significant (Table 4): Biology task persistence χ2 = 733.15 (p < .001); Physics task persistence χ2 = 591.41 (p < .001). Patterns: Biology persistence was highest in Adaptive and Biology-Adaptive; Moderate was higher than Indifferent, Maladaptive, and Physics-Adaptive; Maladaptive was lower than Physics-Adaptive. Physics persistence was highest in Adaptive and Physics-Adaptive; Moderate was higher than Indifferent, Maladaptive, and Biology-Adaptive. Additional analysis (Gender composition across motivational profiles): Configural Frequency Analysis (Bonferroni-adjusted) showed significant gender differences: Indifferent profile had more boys and fewer girls than expected (χ2 = 8.19, p = 0.005). Physics-Adaptive had more boys and fewer girls (χ2 = 7.29, p = 0.005). Biology-Adaptive had more girls and fewer boys (χ2 = 12.86, p = 0.0003). Other profiles did not differ in gender composition. Additional analysis (Perceived teacher need-supportive and need-thwarting behavior across profiles): Omnibus group differences across profiles were significant for all teacher-perception outcomes (Table 4): Biology need-supportive behavior χ2 = 172.35 (p < .001); Biology need-thwarting behavior χ2 = 61.68 (p < .001); Physics need-supportive behavior χ2 = 282.31 (p < .001); Physics need-thwarting behavior χ2 = 151.38 (p < .001). Profile-specific patterns: Biology need-support was higher in Biology-Adaptive and Adaptive; Indifferent and Maladaptive perceived lower biology need-support. Physics need-support was lower in Indifferent, Maladaptive, and Biology-Adaptive; higher in Physics-Adaptive and Adaptive. Maladaptive perceived higher biology need-thwarting; Indifferent/Physics-Adaptive/Adaptive perceived lower physics need-thwarting.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Estonia Grade 8–9 biology and physics motivational profile the study leveraged motivational profile membership to predict reported deep learning strategy use, finding that students in the Adaptive profile used deep strategies more and students in the Indifferent profile used them least, with Maladaptive also showing reduced deep strategy use. This indicates that strengthening students’ expectancy/value/cost profiles may promote the adoption of deep learning strategies, informing instructional interventions that explicitly teach and scaffold deep learning while addressing motivational vulnerabilities.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a school-based assessment in Estonia (34 schools; N=1502; Grades 8–9) to identify latent expectancy–value–cost motivational profiles in biology and physics and to examine how these profiles relate to gender, perceived teacher need-support/need-thwarting, task persistence, and deep learning strategy use. The authors estimated a latent profile analysis with TYPE = COMPLEX clustered by classroom and selected a six-profile solution using AIC/BIC/aBIC, entropy (0.81), and VLMR (0.199). They found that most students belonged to subject-general profiles (Moderate 41%, Adaptive 30%, Maladaptive 9%, Indifferent 3%), while smaller subject-specific profiles existed (Biology-Adaptive 9%, Physics-Adaptive 8%). Significant profile differences emerged for teacher perceptions (all omnibus χ2 p<.001), task persistence (biology χ2=733.15; physics χ2=591.41), and deep strategy use (χ2=124.97). Limitations include reliance on self-report measures, voluntary participation, and no reported missing-data handling; results are cross-sectional, so motivational–behavior associations cannot be interpreted causally.
